title: Round 5 - the horizon ladder
focus: Every window measured in rounds 1 through 4 was between 45 and 284 sessions long. Does the ranking depend on how long the competition holds cards open, six months versus ten years, separate from the regime-mix question round 4 had just answered?
headline: The best annualized figure in the field falls from +31.6% at one year to +7.6% at ten years - the same cards, the same engine, the same metric, the same calendar.
outcome:
Fifteen cards, round 4's field plus A-rotation reinstated, were run across 27 windows: a 21-window ladder sampled evenly at five horizons from six months to ten years, plus a separate 6-window bear arm never pooled into the ladder's medians. The card leading the field at six months and one year, A-rotation, fell to rank 5 of 15 at ten years.

The variant experiments that had occupied three prior rounds measured essentially nothing at a long hold: B2-hold-90 differed from B-momentum by nearly twelve points at one year and was inside half a point of it at ten, confirming that the whole take-profit/max-hold axis had mostly been measuring the length of the window rather than the merit of the rule.

The bear arm identified the field's real hedges by inverting the ladder ranking: c20-rotation, last of fifteen at every ladder horizon, was first in the bear arm, a swing large enough to read as an unlabelled hedge rather than a failed strategy.

Re-deriving every ladder result against QQQ instead of SPY left the ordering largely unchanged but roughly halved the magnitudes - for a field of AI and semiconductor-heavy books, QQQ is the more demanding and more relevant benchmark.

The caveat that limits every figure in the round: every top card's universe was chosen by an analyst writing in 2026 and then run backward from 2013, a decade in which knowing which semiconductor names to hold was worth the most, and the programme's survivorship gate does not catch a thesis-picked basket the way it catches a mechanically index-derived one. Every long-rung figure is stated as an upper bound for this reason.
carries_forward: Every long-horizon figure in this round is an upper bound, since analysts picked 2026-era winners and ran them backward from 2013, and the survivorship gate does not catch thesis-picked baskets.
The take-profit/max-hold-days variant axis is effectively unmeasurable at a multi-year hold and should stay closed.
QQQ should be used alongside SPY as a benchmark for AI/semiconductor-heavy books, since it roughly halves their apparent edge without much reordering the field.
The bear arm and the ladder ranking mostly disagree on which cards are hedges, so round 6's paper-desk selection needs to weigh both rather than the ladder alone.
